# OPERATIONS IMPROVEMENT PLAN: COMPRESSING LEAD TIME WITHOUT SACRIFICING QUALITY

## EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The company is losing market share to a competitor with 57% faster lead times. Previous compression attempts failed because they removed quality checkpoints, not because speed and quality are fundamentally incompatible. The real problem is that **time is trapped in sequential, batched, and approval-dependent processes**—not in the actual production steps.

This plan identifies where time actually lives, redesigns workflow to move work in parallel rather than series, rebuilds quality as a real-time gate (not a post-production inspection), and creates aligned accountability across Production, Quality, and Sales that replaces blame-sharing with joint success metrics.

**Expected outcome:** 6-week quoted lead time (down from 14) without quality regression, achieved through process redesign, not corner-cutting.

---

## SECTION 1: DIAGNOSTIC—WHERE IS THE TIME ACTUALLY LOST?

### 1.1 Current State Value Stream Analysis

Before designing solutions, you must see reality, not assumptions. Schedule a production walkthrough with cross-functional observers.

```
CURRENT 14-WEEK LEAD TIME: WHERE IT ACTUALLY GOES
═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

VISIBLE/EASY TIME (What everyone sees):
├─ Raw material procurement: 2 weeks
├─ Assembly/machining: 3-4 weeks (actual production)
├─ Final inspection: 1 week
├─ Packaging/logistics: 1 week
│
└─ Subtotal visible: ~7-9 weeks

HIDDEN/WASTED TIME (Where 5-7 weeks disappears):
├─ Time Category A: WAITING FOR APPROVAL/HANDOFF
│  ├─ Order enters system → Wait for production scheduling: 2-3 days
│  ├─ Design/engineering review before production: 3-5 days
│  ├─ Quality approves BOM/process: 2-3 days
│  ├─ After each major stage, wait for next stage to be ready: 2-3 days per handoff
│  ├─ Sales approval (does customer want customizations?): 1-2 days
│  ├─ Subtotal: ~2 weeks of pure waiting
│
├─ Time Category B: BATCHING & SCHEDULING INEFFICIENCY
│  ├─ Jobs sit in queue until production batch is full: 2-3 days average
│  ├─ Quality department batches inspections (inspects 10 units at once): 1-2 days delay
│  ├─ Shipping waits for 5 units to fill pallet: 1-2 days
│  ├─ Subtotal: ~1 week of batching delays
│
├─ Time Category C: SEQUENTIAL QUALITY INSPECTIONS (WASTEFUL)
│  ├─ Inspection 1 (raw materials): After materials arrive, before assembly
│  │  └─ Wait for inspection queue + actual inspection: 2-3 days (no urgency)
│  ├─ Inspection 2 (mid-production checkpoint): After step 5 of 8
│  │  └─ Problem: If flaw found here, 5 prior steps rework needed
│  │  └─ Creates rework, delays, quality issues
│  └─ Inspection 3 (final): After all assembly
│      └─ If major flaw found (happens 2-3% of the time), unit rejected = weeks lost
│
├─ Time Category D: REWORK & QUALITY ESCAPES
│  ├─ Baseline rework rate: 5-8% of units need some rework
│  ├─ Average rework cycle: 2-4 days (unit goes back to relevant station, waits in queue, reworked, re-inspected)
│  ├─ Quality escapes (defects found by customer): 0.5-1% → months of warranty, reputation damage
│  └─ Impact on lead time: Every percentage point of rework adds 3-5 days to average
│
├─ Time Category E: SUPPLIER DEPENDENCIES & MATERIAL DELAYS
│  ├─ Critical sub-assemblies ordered 4 weeks in advance (safety stock)
│  ├─ If supplier late (happens 1 in 4 times), entire order delayed
│  ├─ Alternative suppliers exist but require qualification (2-week process)
│  └─ No visibility into supplier production schedules
│
└─ Time Category F: SALES/CUSTOMER-SIDE DELAYS
   ├─ Customer takes 3-5 days to provide final specs/approvals
   ├─ Sales forwards to engineering; engineering queues it (2-3 days)
   ├─ Sales doesn't enforce deadlines (fearful of losing customer)
   └─ Compressed into "waiting" but actually controllable

TOTAL WASTED TIME: 5-7 WEEKS (of 14 weeks total)
═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

KEY INSIGHT:
The competitor isn't faster because they've figured out how to assemble faster.
They're faster because they've eliminated the waiting, batching, and sequential inspection delays.
They likely have similar production cycle time (3-4 weeks) but have compressed everything else to 2-3 weeks.
```

### 1.2 Root Cause Analysis: Why Did Previous Speed-Up Attempts Fail?

```
WHAT WENT WRONG LAST TIME: THE WARRANTY SPIKE INCIDENT
═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

WHAT WAS ATTEMPTED:
├─ Removed the mid-production inspection (Inspection #2)
├─ Rationale: "Saves time; if there's a flaw, we'll catch it at final inspection"
├─ Expected result: Save 2-3 days per unit
└─ Actual result: Warranty claims spiked 40%, took 2 years to recover

WHY THIS APPROACH FAILED (The Real Problem):
├─ Flaw #1: Removed quality gate without improving upstream quality
│  ├─ Quality was not "built in" to production; it was "inspected in"
│  ├─ Removing inspection didn't improve production; it just hid defects longer
│  ├─ When defect was only caught at final inspection, it required reworking all prior steps
│  ├─ This meant final inspection delays skyrocketed (each bad unit takes hours)
│  └─ Plus customer escapes (defects that made it through final inspection)
│
├─ Flaw #2: Didn't address the real source of defects
│  ├─ Defects came from: Assembly procedures, operator training, component variations, tool wear
│  ├─ Speed-up tried to skip the finding, not fix the causing
│  └─ Like removing smoke detectors to make a house go faster
│
├─ Flaw #3: Misaligned incentives during the change
│  ├─ Production incentive: "Speed" (remove inspections)
│  ├─ Quality incentive: "No defects" (need inspections)
│  ├─ Sales incentive: "Deliver on time" (rush production)
│  ├─ Result: Production and Sales aligned to skip Quality
│  └─ Quality had no power to prevent it; just documented the mess afterward
│
└─ LESSON LEARNED:
   Speed and quality aren't trade-offs if you redesign the PROCESS.
   But if you just compress the old process, you'll sacrifice quality.

WHAT NOT TO REPEAT:
├─ Don't remove quality gates; move them upstream
├─ Don't trust inspection catches errors created by broken processes
├─ Don't align Sales/Production incentives against Quality
├─ Don't expect speed improvements without process redesign
└─ Don't skip root-cause fixes in favor of schedule compression
```

## SECTION 2: REDESIGN STRATEGY—COMPRESS TIME WITHOUT REMOVING QUALITY

### 2.1 Core Principle: Parallel vs. Sequential Work

```
THE FUNDAMENTAL SHIFT: FROM SERIAL TO PARALLEL PROCESS
═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

CURRENT (SERIAL) FLOW:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                            │
│  Step 1:        Step 2:        Step 3:        Step 4:        Step 5:     │
│  Order in       Design &       Raw material   Assembly       Inspection  │
│  queue          Approval       Procurement    & Production   & QA         │
│  (2-3 days)     (3-5 days)     (2 weeks)      (3-4 weeks)   (1+ weeks)  │
│                                                                            │
│  ────→ WAIT ────→ WAIT ────→ WAIT ────→ WAIT ────→ WAIT ────→           │
│                                                                            │
│  Total Time: 14 weeks (each step waits for previous to finish)           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

REDESIGNED (PARALLEL) FLOW:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Design & Approval             Raw Material Procurement  Assembly        │
│  (Start immediately)           (Start immediately)       (Start when     │
│  2-3 days                      2 weeks                   materials      │
│                                                          arrive)        │
│  ──┐                           ┌──→ Supplier 1 ──┐                     │
│    │                           │                 │                      │
│    ├──→ Fast approval ──→ Fast supplier ├──→ Fast assembly ──→ Quality  │
│    │                           │                 │          Gate        │
│    └──→ Check design ──────────┼──→ Supplier 2 ──┘          (Real-time) │
│       for manufacturing        │                                        │
│       constraints              └──→ Component checking                  │
│       (in parallel with                 (incoming inspection)            │
│        sourcing)                                                         │
│                                                                          │
│  Total Time: 6 weeks (overlapped steps; bottleneck is now material wait)│
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

TIME COMPRESSION MECHANISMS:
═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

MECHANISM 1: PARALLELIZATION
├─ Design approval and material procurement happen simultaneously (not sequentially)
├─ Engineering validates design for manufacturability WHILE sourcing identifies suppliers
├─ Saves: 2-3 weeks (no longer waiting for design before ordering materials)
├─ Risk mitigation: Design review must be "complete enough" for sourcing, not "perfect"
│  ├─ Criteria: CAD drawings done, material specs defined, manufacturing process sketched
│  ├─ Not required: Every detail finalized, cost optimized, supplier negotiated
│  └─ Philosophy: "Rough in, refine in parallel" vs. "Perfect before starting"

MECHANISM 2: REAL-TIME QUALITY GATES (NOT POST-PRODUCTION INSPECTION)
├─ Move quality checks to occur DURING assembly, not after
├─ Incoming material inspection happens within 4 hours (priority queue, not batched)
├─ Assembly checkpoints: After every 2-3 critical steps, quality technician spot-checks
├─ Example: Unit on assembly line; at checkpoint, technician checks [specific dimension]
│  ├─ Takes 5 minutes; happens in real-time
│  ├─ If OK, unit moves forward immediately
│  ├─ If flaw, caught immediately with rework scope defined
│  └─ No batching delays; no surprise failures at end
├─ Saves: 3-5 days (no separate final inspection queue)
└─ Improves quality: Issues caught early, when rework is minimal

MECHANISM 3: SUPPLIER AGILITY
├─ Develop 2-3 qualified suppliers for every critical component (instead of 1)
├─ Create standing purchase agreements: "When we order, delivery in 1 week" (not 2-3 weeks)
├─ This requires: Supplier capability + your volume commitment + their capacity reservation
├─ Saves: 1-2 weeks (shorter and more reliable material lead times)
├─ Backup supplier reduces supply risk (one supplier late doesn't stop entire order)

MECHANISM 4: BATCH-SIZE REDUCTION
├─ Current: Wait until 10 units are ready for inspection, then inspect them all
├─ Redesigned: Inspect each unit immediately after it completes a stage (batch of 1)
├─ This requires: Staffing inspection differently
│  ├─ Instead of 1 inspector batching 10 units on Tuesdays
│  ├─ Use rotating inspectors or cross-trained team members checking continuously
│  └─ Total inspection hours same; spread across time instead of concentrated
├─ Saves: 1-2 days (no batching delays; immediate feedback)
└─ Improves quality: Defects found immediately; root cause caught fresh

MECHANISM 5: CUSTOMER DECISION FORCING
├─ Current: Sales collects specs over 3-5 days; doesn't enforce deadlines
├─ Redesigned: Customer provides specs in 24 hours, or order uses standard config
│  ├─ This is a SERVICE, not a constraint
│  ├─ "We can deliver standard [model] in 5 weeks; custom in 8 weeks"
│  ├─ Forces customer decision immediately
│  └─ Eliminates the longest delays (customer indecision)
├─ Saves: 2-3 days (parallelized with procurement; more importantly, removes customer delays)

MECHANISM 6: ELIMINATING REWORK DELAYS
├─ Current: Rework happens ad-hoc; waits in queue; can take 2-4 days
├─ Redesigned: Rework happens same-day or next-day (dedicated slot, rapid turnaround)
│  ├─ Quality technician identifies rework need; routes to correct station immediately
│  ├─ Station schedules it in next available slot (not when batch of 5 others is ready)
│  └─ Re-inspection happens same day
├─ Saves: 1-2 days per rework incident
└─ Improves quality: Root cause identified and fixed immediately (before next unit)
```

### 2.2 Specific Process Redesigns by Function

```
PRODUCTION PROCESS REDESIGN: FROM BATCH TO FLOW
═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

CURRENT PRODUCTION FLOW (BATCHED):
├─ Job enters system
├─ Waits in queue until production scheduler has 5-10 similar jobs
├─ Batch scheduled for specific production slot (determined weekly)
├─ Jobs move through stations as a batch
├─ Finished batch waits for next stage (quality inspection)
└─ Lead time variability: 10-18 weeks depending on queue

REDESIGNED PRODUCTION FLOW (CONTINUOUS WITH PRIORITY):
├─ Job enters system immediately
├─ Classified into priority tier:
│  ├─ Tier 1 (Express): Standard configuration, no customization (5-week quote)
│  │  └─ Moves immediately to assembly line; no waiting for batch
│  ├─ Tier 2 (Fast-track): Standard with minor options (6-week quote)
│  │  └─ Queued but prioritized; starts within 1-2 days
│  └─ Tier 3 (Custom): Non-standard, requires engineering (8-week quote)
│      └─ Engineering queue; starts within 3-5 days
├─ Express jobs get dedicated slots on the assembly line (e.g., Mondays, Wednesdays)
│  ├─ Reduces context-switching; operators familiar with that configuration
│  ├─ Materials pre-positioned; tools set up correctly
│  └─ Rework rare because of familiarity
├─ Intermediate batch sizes: Instead of 10, do 3-4 units
│  ├─ Smaller batches move through faster
│  ├─ Quality gates don't have to wait for full batch
│  └─ Utilization nearly same; lead time cut in half
└─ Lead time predictability: Tier 1 = 5 weeks ±3 days; Tier 2 = 6 ±5 days

STAFFING IMPLICATIONS:
├─ Production scheduling complexity increases (more frequent starts)
│  └─ Mitigation: Use scheduling software (SOP, APS systems)
├─ Production floor discipline required (reduce context-switching losses)
│  └─ Mitigation: Dedicated slots + operator training + visual management
├─ Rework response time critical (can't let rework sit in queue)
│  └─ Mitigation: Floating technicians assigned to rework (not tied to specific station)

SUPPLY CHAIN/PROCUREMENT REDESIGN: FROM LONG LEAD TO RESPONSIVE
═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

CURRENT SUPPLY CHAIN (PUSH-BASED):
├─ Forecast demand 8-10 weeks out
├─ Order materials in bulk (2-4 week lead time + safety stock)
├─ Materials arrive in batches; sit in inventory
├─ Production pulls from inventory when jobs scheduled
├─ Problem: Forecasts wrong; inventory expensive; long lead times

REDESIGNED SUPPLY CHAIN (PULL-BASED WITH SHORT LEAD TIMES):
├─ Partner with 2-3 suppliers for every critical component
│  ├─ Each supplier qualified and capable of 1-week delivery
│  ├─ Requires: Supplier agreement to keep safety stock for you
│  ├─ Cost: You compensate them slightly (1-2% price premium) for carrying stock
│  └─ Benefit: You reduce your lead time from 4 weeks to 1 week per component
│
├─ When job enters production (not 8 weeks ahead), trigger purchase orders
│  ├─ Supplier pulls from their safety stock; ships in 1 week
│  ├─ Timing: Order placed on Day 2-3 of 6-week cycle; materials arrive by Day 9-10
│  ├─ Production starts Day 8-10 (materials arrive just before needed)
│  └─ Inventory in your facility drops by 50%+ (less buffer needed)
│
├─ Standard components ordered in small batch sizes (3-4 units, not 10)
│  └─ Matches production batch sizes; less inventory sitting around
│
├─ "Expedite supplier" arrangement:
│  ├─ If your forecast shortens (customer wants faster delivery), supplier is prepared
│  ├─ Cost: Premium (10-15% higher price) for 3-day emergency delivery
│  ├─ Occasionally needed; enables "premium fast delivery" service to customers
│  └─ Treated as margin opportunity, not cost burden
│
└─ Supply visibility: Real-time tracking of supplier production + shipment

SUPPLIER PARTNERSHIP MODEL:
├─ Current state: Adversarial; lowest-price bidding; high turnover
├─ Redesigned state: Partnership; stable demand; collaborative improvement
│
├─ Supplier Selection Criteria:
│  ├─ Capability: Can deliver 1-week cycle time? Yes = qualified
│  ├─ Reliability: Track record of on-time delivery? >95% = partner
│  ├─ Responsiveness: Willing to work on 1-week windows? Yes = included
│  └─ Quality: Can hit your spec without incoming inspection? 99%+ = preferred
│
├─ Supplier Contract Structure:
│  ├─ Volume commitment from you (minimum monthly purchase)
│  ├─ Response guarantee from supplier (1-week delivery promised)
│  ├─ Price: 2-5% premium over bulk-order pricing (for their rapid-response cost)
│  ├─ Quality: Incoming inspection reduced 50% (supplier quality improving)
│  └─ Collaboration: Quarterly reviews; continuous improvement projects
│
├─ Risk Mitigation:
│  ├─ Dual-source critical components (if Supplier A late, Supplier B covers)
│  ├─ Safety stock maintained only for long-lead items (rare exotic materials)
│  └─ Strategic inventory of most common components (covers 2 weeks of sales)
│
└─ Supplier Development Roadmap:
   ├─ Current: 1-2 suppliers per component
   ├─ Month 1-3: Qualify 2nd supplier (parallel)
   ├─ Month 4-6: Negotiate 1-week lead time agreement
   ├─ Month 7-9: Reduce your buffer inventory; test responsiveness
   └─ Month 10-12: Optimize pricing and performance

MATERIAL FLOW TIMELINE (REDESIGNED):
```
Day 1-2:     Customer order received; specs finalized
Day 3:       Purchase orders triggered with 2-3 suppliers
Day 4-5:     Engineering reviews design for manufacturability
Day 6-8:     Materials in transit from suppliers
Day 8:       Production slot scheduled; pre-production setup
Day 9-11:    Materials arrive; receiving inspection (fast-track)
Day 12-35:   Assembly + real-time quality gates (3-4 weeks)
Day 36:      Final quality gate (pass/fail check)
Day 37-39:   Packaging + logistics
Day 40-42:   Delivery window (6 weeks, give or take 2 days)
```

QUALITY REDESIGN: FROM POST-PRODUCTION INSPECTION TO IN-PROCESS GATES
═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

CURRENT QUALITY MODEL (DETECTIVE):
├─ Quality checks happen AFTER production is complete
├─ Process: Finish assembly → Wait for inspection queue → Inspect (1-2 days)
├─ If defect found: Rework queue → Wait for rework → Re-inspect
├─ Philosophy: "Inspect quality in" (inspection creates quality)
├─ Problems:
│  ├─ Defects cost maximum to fix (rework entire unit)
│  ├─ Customer escapes possible (some defects slip through)
│  ├─ Inspection queue creates 2-3 day delays
│  └─ Root causes not addressed; same defects repeat

REDESIGNED QUALITY MODEL (PREVENTIVE):
├─ Quality checks happen DURING production (in real-time)
├─ Process: Assembly step → Immediate checkpoint → Pass/Fail → Move forward or rework immediately
├─ Philosophy: "Build quality in" (prevent defects from happening)
├─ Implementation:

QUALITY GATE LOCATIONS & PROCEDURES:
├─ Gate 1: Incoming Material Check (When materials arrive, not 2 days later)
│  ├─ Time: 1-2 hours; single unit sample inspection
│  ├─ What's checked: Critical dimensions, material properties, visual defects
│  ├─ Output: Pass → Move to kitting station; Fail → Contact supplier; replacement ordered
│  ├─ Staffing: Dedicated incoming quality person (shifts: 6am-2pm, 2pm-10pm)
│  └─ Benefit: Defective materials caught immediately; no assembly wasted
│
├─ Gate 2: Pre-Assembly Check (After materials kitted, before assembly starts)
│  ├─ Time: 30 minutes; ensure all materials present + correct
│  ├─ What's checked: BOM accuracy, right quantities, correct specs
│  ├─ Output: Pass → Unit authorized for assembly start
│  └─ Benefit: Prevents stoppage mid-assembly due to missing parts
│
├─ Gate 3: Mid-Assembly Checkpoint #1 (After assembly step 3)
│  ├─ Time: 15 minutes; spot check critical assembly points
│  ├─ What's checked: Alignment, fastening torque, sealant application
│  ├─ Output: Pass → Proceed to next station; Fail → Immediate rework (same day)
│  ├─ Staffing: Roving quality technician (covers 2-3 assembly stations)
│  └─ Benefit: Defects caught early; rework minimal (only 3 steps to redo, not 8)
│
├─ Gate 4: Mid-Assembly Checkpoint #2 (After assembly step 6)
│  ├─ Time: 20 minutes; spot check next critical points
│  ├─ What's checked: Testing of sub-assemblies, calibration, fit & function
│  ├─ Output: Pass → Final assembly; Fail → Quick rework + re-test
│  └─ Benefit: Catch functional issues before final assembly
│
├─ Gate 5: Final Assembly Check (Before packaging; after all steps)
│  ├─ Time: 30 minutes; comprehensive final functional test
│  ├─ What's checked: All performance specs, safety features, visual quality
│  ├─ Output: Pass → Approved for packaging; Fail → Root cause analysis + rework
│  ├─ Staffing: Senior quality inspector (most experienced)
│  └─ Benefit: Gate-keeper for customer quality; prevents escapes
│
└─ Gate 6: Post-Packaging Check (Random sampling; 5-10% of units)
   ├─ Time: 15 minutes; ensure packaging intact + label correct
   ├─ Purpose: Catch any post-assembly handling damage
   └─ Benefit: Assurance that quality maintained through final step

QUALITY GATE STAFFING MODEL:
├─ Current: 3-4 quality inspectors; work 8am-5pm; batch inspection 2x/week
├─ Redesigned: 5-6 quality technicians; rotating shifts (6am-2pm, 2pm-10pm, 10pm-6am)
│  ├─ Each technician assigned to 2-3 production lines
│  ├─ Technician stays in area; immediate response to issues
│  ├─ Cross-training so any technician can cover any gate
│  └─ Net staffing increase: 1-2 people (offset by elimination of large batch inspections)
│
├─ Technician Role Evolution:
│  ├─ Old: "Inspector" (check finished product; say pass/fail)
│  ├─ New: "Quality coach" (check in-process; teach operators; identify root causes)
│  ├─ Distinction: Proactive vs. reactive
│  └─ Skills needed: Technical knowledge + teaching + problem-solving (not just pass/fail)

QUALITY METRIC CHANGES:
├─ Current metrics:
│  ├─ % of units passing final inspection
│  ├─ Warranty claim rate (lagging indicator; measured months later)
│  └─ Rework hours per unit (reactive)
│
├─ Redesigned metrics:
│  ├─ First-pass yield at each gate (% of units passing without rework)
│  ├─ Lead time from defect finding to root cause fix (speed of learning)
│  ├─ Defect rate trend (month-over-month; improving?)
│  ├─ Operator quality awareness (survey; do operators understand quality specs?)
│  └─ Supplier quality performance (% of incoming materials meeting spec without inspection)

ROOT CAUSE PROBLEM-SOLVING SYSTEM:
├─ Every time a defect is found:
│  ├─ Quality technician conducts 5-why root cause analysis (same shift, if possible)
│  ├─ Output: "This happened because [root cause], which we fix by [action]"
│  ├─ Action assigned to: Operator, supervisor, engineer, or supplier (whoever owns the cause)
│  └─ Follow-up: Action taken within 3-5 days; verified in next 10 units
│
├─ Monthly quality review:
│  ├─ Top 5 defect types analyzed
│  ├─ Trends discussed (increasing/decreasing?)
│  ├─ Actions reviewed (did they work?)
│  └─ Next month's focus areas set
│
└─ Philosophy shift: Quality as continuous learning system, not inspection/compliance ritual

CERTIFICATION & DOCUMENTED PROCEDURES:
├─ Current: Procedures exist; inconsistently followed; no documentation of who did what
├─ Redesigned:
│  ├─ Standard procedure for each assembly station (posted visually)
│  ├─ Each quality gate has documented checklist (what to verify)
│  ├─ Technician documents each check (date, time, results, tech ID)
│  ├─ Traceability: Can see exact quality path of any delivered unit
│  ├─ For certified products: Documentation required for audit trail
│  └─ System: Simple checklist + logging (paper or digital, doesn't matter; consistency matters)
```

### 2.3 Functional Alignment & Accountability

```
ALIGNING PRODUCTION, QUALITY, AND SALES: FROM BLAME TO JOINT SUCCESS
═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

CURRENT STATE: MISALIGNED INCENTIVES & BLAME CULTURE
═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Production Department:
├─ KPI: Schedule adherence (deliver on promised date to customers)
├─ Incentive: Production bonus based on % of on-time deliveries
├─ Problem: Under time pressure, tempted to skip quality checks
├─ Behavior: "We'll deliver on time; if there's a quality issue, that's QA's problem"
├─ Attitude toward Quality: "QA delays us; they're the bottleneck"
└─ Risk: Rushing production, leading to defects that emerge as warranty claims months later

Quality Department:
├─ KPI: Defect rate (% of units passing final inspection without rework)
├─ Incentive: Bonus for catching defects (fewer escapes to customer)
├─ Problem: Incentivized to be thorough, which takes time
├─ Behavior: Long inspection cycles; holds up production; found to be "the bottleneck"
├─ Attitude toward Production: "They rush; we have to catch their mistakes"
├─ Risk: Positioned as safety net, not business partner; seen as cost, not value
└─ Unintended result: Quality gate becomes handoff/approval bottleneck rather than gate

Sales Department:
├─ KPI: Order volume (number of deals closed; revenue)
├─ Incentive: Commission on sales; bonus for % of orders delivered on-time
├─ Problem: Promises customers aggressive delivery to win deals
├─ Behavior: Makes commitments without confirming capacity with Production
├─ Attitude toward Production: "They're the constraint; I can sell more if they go faster"
├─ Risk: Promises impossible dates; creates schedule pressure that forces corner-cutting
└─ Unintended result: Sets expectation (6-week delivery promised) that can't be met; customer frustrated

RESULT OF MISALIGNMENT:
├─ Production under time pressure; cuts corners → defects increase
├─ Quality finding defects; backs up production → delays lengthen
├─ Sales promising fast delivery; Production can't deliver → customer complaints
├─ Blame cycle: Sales blames Production (slow); Production blames Quality (delays them);
│  Quality blames Production (defects them); circle continues
├─ When the previous speed-up attempt failed (warranty spike):
│  ├─ Production said: "Quality should have caught those defects"
│  ├─ Quality said: "We were forced to skip inspections due to time pressure"
│  ├─ Sales said: "This is why we need faster production" (missing the point)
│  └─ CEO: Frustrated with all three; no consensus on how to fix it
└─ Nobody owns "lead time + quality together"; everyone optimizes their own metric

REDESIGNED: SHARED METRICS & ALIGNED ACCOUNTABILITY
═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

PRINCIPLE: Move from individual functional KPIs to shared business outcomes

SHARED OUTCOME METRIC 1: "QUOTED LEAD TIME HIT RATE"
├─ Definition: % of orders delivered within the quoted lead time window
│  ├─ If quoted 6 weeks, delivered in week 5-7 = hit
│  ├─ If quoted 6 weeks, delivered in week 8 = miss
│  └─ If quoted 6 weeks, delivered in week 4 = miss (over-promised)
├─ Ownership: Production (owns schedule) + Sales (owns customer expectation) + Quality (owns cycle time)
├─ Why this metric:
│  ├─ Directly tied to customer satisfaction (most important metric)
│  ├─ Forces Sales to make achievable promises
│  ├─ Forces Production to meet realistic commitments
│  ├─ Forces Quality to find efficiencies, not add delays
│  └─
